overview: The Qarakhanids linked Central Asian cities, mountain routes and Turkic ruling families. Their eastern and western branches followed different political paths. This map’s 1100 to 1200 span and oversized single outline are approximate coverage, not the dynasty’s lifetime or a frontier. Earlier foundations and later conquests appear below as context.

periods.title: Earlier rise
periods.summary: Muslim Turkic rulers expanded; the capture of Bukhara in 999 ended Samanid rule there.

periods.title: Earlier division
periods.summary: Eastern and western khanates emerged. Seljuk intervention subordinated western rulers in 1089.

periods.title: The mapped century
periods.summary: Qara Khitai expansion reduced Qarakhanid independence while local dynastic rulers continued.

periods.title: Later dynastic endings
periods.summary: Eastern and western branches ended through different conquests and political upheavals.

sections.title: A dynasty across cities and caravan routes

items.text: The ruling family treated the realm as a collective inheritance, distributing territories among its members. Around 1040 it divided into western and eastern khanates, associated with Samarkand and with Balasaghun and Kashgar. Several royal relatives could exercise power at once, making a single list of kings misleading.

The Qara Khitai took Balasaghun in 1134 and defeated the Seljuk-led alliance at Qatwan in 1141. Qarakhanid princes still ruled locally under the new overlords. A familiar dynasty could remain on coins even after its freedom to decide policy had shrunk.

Travel to Song China involved paperwork and limits as well as camels. In 1078 the Chinese court restricted a Qarakhanid delegation to fifty people. Duturaeva’s study also identifies an earlier mission lodged at a postal station in Kaifeng, whose delegation included diplomatic and military officers.

Meng Yuanlao’s account of New Year audiences in Kaifeng describes envoys from Khotan arriving with wives and sons. He noticed patterned felt hats, belted robes and camels carrying bags and bronze bells. This specific court scene puts families into the history of long-distance travel; the caravan certainly did not arrive silently.

Excavations at Taraz have exposed residential and commercial buildings, a main street, a water-supply system and caravanserais where travellers could stop. The remains connect the city’s famous trading role with the practical work of maintaining streets, buildings and water. The excavations of 2011 to 2016 added substantially to this picture.

Two bathhouses beneath the area of Taraz’s modern central market were dated to the tenth through twelfth centuries. One uncovered in the 1960s had four rooms, a clay seat and troughs or bathing basins. Bathing required a purpose-built place with fittings, not merely a convenient stretch of river.

Another Taraz bathhouse, excavated in 1938, had richly decorated walls: yellow six- and eight-pointed stars stood against a reddish-brown ground, with stems and leaves nearby. The museum interprets its layout as separate male and female sections. A washing trip could also put a bather in a room full of patterns.

For earlier regional food history, the mountain town of Tashbulak in present-day Uzbekistan offers something better than a guessed menu: ancient food remains. Its ninth- to eleventh-century deposits included peach and grape remains, melon seeds, and walnut and pistachio shells. These finds record foods handled at this particular town.

Tashbulak stood roughly 2,200 metres above sea level, too high for many of the fruit trees represented in its refuse. Researchers infer that lower-elevation communities supplied some of these foods. Mountain-town life depended on connections with farming districts; a peach could have travelled uphill before someone ate it.

The food study sampled a rubbish deposit beside an area interpreted as a bazaar. Researchers used flotation to recover small plant remains from soil, then identified seeds and fragments. A discarded fruit stone can become evidence of trade centuries later. Archaeology sometimes gives the rubbish heap the last word.

A document from 1066, before this map’s century, established an endowment for a hospital serving poor people at Samarkand. It placed the institution south of the main bazaar. This is concrete evidence for organized medical care in the Qarakhanid city, although the document does not supply a complete guide to its treatments.

A second 1066 document supported a madrasa, an institution of learning. The endowments described income-producing properties, many of them caravanserais near the bazaar. Education and care were therefore tied to the city’s commercial property. The college’s precise identification among excavated ruins remains disputed.

Excavated palace pavilions at Samarkand preserve another side of eleventh- and twelfth-century life. Fallen wall paintings included birds, dancers, hunting dogs and guards presenting royal symbols. These were elite settings, but the fragments preserve the work of painters and decorators whose names the royal chronicles rarely celebrate.

At Uzgen, archaeologists uncovered a pottery workshop with four rectangular furnaces dated to the late twelfth century. Firing vessels required a workshop, fuel and careful control of heat. These remains make the craft workers behind city life visible alongside the more conspicuous monuments of their rulers.

Uzgen’s attached brick mausoleums carried carved plaster, terracotta ornament and bands of writing. Their inscriptions include dates in 1152, 1186 and 1187, connecting architecture with the dynasty’s later generations and commanders. The lettering was part of the building’s decoration as well as a way of remembering the dead.

Bukhara’s Kalyan minaret preserves a more personal building record: terracotta inscriptions date construction to 1127 under Arslan Khan and name its builder, Bako. A steep spiral stair runs inside the tower. Its survival gives the medieval skyline a named craftsperson as well as a royal patron.

sections.title: A dictionary and a small sample of writing

items.text: Mahmud of Kashgar completed his compendium of Turkic language in Baghdad in 1074, intending to teach Turkic to Arabic speakers. Its only known surviving manuscript is a later copy completed in 1266, now in Istanbul’s Millet Manuscript Library. The distinction matters: an eleventh-century work can survive in a book copied almost two centuries afterward.

A Qarakhanid copper coin in the Ashmolean bears the Arabic words محمد رسول الله, meaning “Muḥammad is the messenger of God.” The museum dates it to before 1178 and attributes it to Sulayman Tafghaj Khan. This is Arabic religious writing on a dynasty’s coin, not a sample of Turkic speech; the short excerpt joins the inscription’s line breaks.

ending.text: The map stops in 1200, before the final dynastic losses. The eastern restoration attempt failed in 1211; Khwarazmian expansion extinguished western and Ferghana rule in 1212-13. These political endings did not erase the region’s towns, communities or Turkic literary traditions.
